title: RepoNorm: teaching coding agents a project's unwritten rules
topic: Quality and trust in AI-written code

sources.title: Acquiring and Verifying Repository Norms for Coding Agents
sources.authors: Kaifeng He, Xiaojun Zhang, Zhenxi Chen, Christoph Treude, Mingwei Liu

summary_md:
**In one sentence:** AI coding agents often write code that passes its tests but still breaks a project's
unwritten rules (a missing test, changelog line or safety step). **RepoNorm** (He et al., 2026) collects those rules
from a project *before* any task, checks each one against the code, and hands the agent only the well-supported ones.

### First, two words
- A **repository** is the shared folder of a software project: all its code, tests, documentation and the full history
  of every change (kept with a tool called Git).
- **Norms** are the team's expectations about *how* a change should be made: "add a test", "write a line in the
  changelog", "keep the existing error handling". Like the house rules in a new job, some are written in a handbook
  (a *contribution guide*); many are unwritten and you only learn them by watching how things are already done.

### The problem
An agent is usually judged by **functional tests**: does the new feature work? In the paper's Jinja example, an agent
passed all 171 functional checks but forgot the changelog entry that the contribution guide requires. In Tiktoken, an
agent passed all 18 checks but skipped an existing repair step for unusual characters in its new code path.
Hand-written instruction files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) help but take effort; generated wikis such as CodeWiki explain the
code but do not say which statements are *obligations*.

### The idea
1. **Explicit channel:** read what the project states (guides, configuration files, automated workflows).
2. **Implicit channel:** infer conventions from what the code consistently does, then test the guess on all matching code
   and look for **counterexamples**. (A rule about Jinja filters was narrowed after the `sum` and `join` filters did not fit.)
3. **Verification:** each candidate is *accepted*, sent for *review* or *rejected*. Git history may be consulted, but
   history alone can never accept or reject a rule.
4. **Delivery:** accepted norms go into a small package of Markdown files ordered by folder, so the agent can look up
   the rules for the files it is changing.

### Results (121 tasks, six small Python projects, three models: DeepSeek, Qwen, Gemini)
| Measure (vs. no guidance, relative change) | RepoNorm |
|---|---|
| All norms followed | +7.42% to +10.77% |
| Contribution norms (tests, docs, changelog, style, typing) | +31.64% to +45.44% |
| Norms the task never mentioned | +11.34% to +17.69% |
| Behaviour norms | already 87.6-96.5% without help; small, mixed changes |

- Functional success was 5.79-9.09 percentage points higher, but **not statistically significant**.
- CodeWiki documentation did not consistently raise compliance.
- Precision: 258 of 300 sampled accepted norms (86%) were correct, but they fully covered only 21.88% of the 160
  reference norms (52.50% after an extra automated review, with precision falling to 75.17%).
- Cost: about 9 minutes per package; 2.14 hours in total, 3.2% of the agents' coding time.

### Why it matters
Trust in AI-written code depends on more than "it works". Reviewers reject changes that ignore the team's conventions.
Giving an agent checked rules *with their evidence* makes its work more complete.

### Limitations
Only Python; six relatively small projects; packages can go stale as the code changes; and the agent may still
overlook relevant rules among many entries.

### IELTS angle
Useful words from the passage: *lapse*, *trivial*, *undermine confidence*, *precaution*, *premature*, *modest*,
*twofold*. In Task 2 essays on work, migration or education, this is a vivid example of how **unwritten rules** trip
up newcomers, and of the benefit of making expectations explicit, with reasons.

discussion: When people start a new job or move to a new country, how do they usually learn the unwritten rules?
Would you trust code, or any other work, produced by an AI if it worked correctly but did not follow your team's usual way of doing things? Why?
Is it better for an organisation to write all its rules down, or are some rules better left unwritten?

parts.title: Learning the House Rules: Can AI Coding Agents Follow a Team's Norms?
parts.passage_html:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-14, which are based on the Reading Passage below.

A Anyone who has started a new job knows that the staff handbook tells only part of the story. It may explain how to claim expenses, but not that the manager expects to be copied into client emails. Newcomers learn these house rules slowly, by watching colleagues. Software teams work in much the same way. Their shared work lives in a repository: a central store holding a project's code, tests and documentation, with a record of every change. Around that code grows a set of norms: expectations about how a change should be made, tested and described. Some are written in a contribution guide; others are visible only in the existing code.

B Increasingly, the newcomer is not a person but an AI coding agent, a program that can explore a repository, edit files and run tests by itself. Such agents are judged mainly on whether their code passes functional tests, which check only that the requested feature works. A 2026 paper by Kaifeng He and colleagues in China and Singapore shows why this is not enough. In one example, an agent asked to extend a feature of Jinja, a Python templating library, passed all 171 functional checks. Yet it did not add an entry to the changelog, the list of changes that Jinja's contribution guide requires, which the task description had not mentioned. Such lapses may look trivial, but they are precisely what slows down human review and undermines confidence in code written by machines.

C A second case is subtler. Tiktoken, a library that prepares text for language models, contains a step that repairs certain unusual characters before passing them to its core encoder. When an agent added a way of processing text in chunks, its new code skipped that repair. The patch passed all 18 functional checks, yet it quietly broke an established behaviour. An agent, then, must both discover norms that the task never mentions and work out where each one applies.

D Existing remedies only partly solve the problem. Developers can write instruction files, such as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, but writing them by hand means identifying every relevant norm and when it applies. Documentation tools such as CodeWiki describe how a repository is organised, yet they leave the agent to decide which statements are obligations and which are merely descriptions. The authors also cite an earlier study which found that agents generally obey instruction files, but without a consistent gain in the number of tasks they solve. Obedience, in other words, is only as useful as the instructions themselves.

E The authors' system, RepoNorm, gathers candidate norms before any task begins, through two channels. The explicit channel reads what the project states in writing, such as contribution guides and configuration files. The implicit channel infers conventions from what the code consistently does, and tests each guess against the code. In Jinja, several filters return a special 'undefined' value for empty input, suggesting that every filter reducing a sequence to one value behaves this way. Checking the matching functions revealed counterexamples: the sum filter returns a starting value, normally zero, and the join filter returns an empty string. The rule was therefore narrowed to filters that select a single element, such as first, last and max.

F Every candidate is then verified and either accepted, sent for review or rejected. RepoNorm can also search the project's history of changes, but historical evidence alone can never accept or reject a norm. This seems a wise precaution, since a once-common practice may have been abandoned. By default only accepted norms reach the agent. They are delivered as plain text files, organised according to the folders they apply to, together with the evidence behind them.

G The researchers tested three AI models, from DeepSeek, Qwen and Gemini, on 121 tasks from six relatively small Python projects, with no extra guidance, with CodeWiki documentation, or with a RepoNorm package. With the package, the share of applicable norms that agents followed rose by between 7.42% and 10.77% in relative terms. The largest gains, of 31.64% to 45.44%, came in contribution norms such as writing tests and updating documentation and changelogs, which functional tests do not check. By contrast, norms about how the code behaves were already followed between 87.6% and 96.5% of the time without help, and changed little. CodeWiki brought no consistent improvement.

H Whether the code worked better is less clear. Functional success rose by between 5.79 and 9.09 percentage points, but none of these differences passed the authors' test of statistical significance. It would therefore be premature to claim that knowing a team's norms makes an agent's code more likely to work; what the study does show is that the code becomes more complete. The norms were largely reliable: of a sample of 300 accepted entries, 258, or 86%, were judged correct. Coverage was weaker: the accepted norms fully captured only 21.88% of 160 reference norms prepared by the researchers.

I The cost is modest. Building a package took just over nine minutes on average, and the total of 2.14 hours was only 3.2% of the time the agents then spent coding. The limitations are equally clear: only Python is supported so far, packages can become out of date as a project changes, and whether the approach works for much larger projects remains untested. Even so, the central lesson applies well beyond software. A newcomer who is shown the house rules, together with the reasons for them, is far more likely to behave like a colleague than like a stranger.

groups.content_html:
How RepoNorm prepares guidance for a coding agent

Before any task is given, RepoNorm collects possible norms in two ways. Some come from what the project says in writing, such as its contribution guide, while others are {{10}} from regular patterns in the code. Each proposed rule is checked against the code, and if {{11}} are found, the rule may be made narrower. Every candidate is then given a status, and normally only norms that have been {{12}} are handed to the agent. These are supplied as plain text files grouped by the {{13}} they cover, so the agent can find the guidance for the part of the project it is changing.

writing.prompt:
When people join a new group, such as a workplace, a school or a country, they often find that many of its rules are unwritten. Some people believe that it is the newcomer's responsibility to learn and adapt to these unwritten rules. Others argue that groups should make their rules clear and explicit for everyone.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

The chart below shows the percentage of a software project's rules (norms) that an AI coding assistant followed when it was given three different kinds of help, for four types of rule. Contribution rules include adding tests and updating documentation; behavioural rules concern how the code must work.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
writing.image_description: Grouped bar chart, percentage of applicable project norms followed (norm compliance rate, 0-100%) by one AI coding model (DeepSeek V4 Flash) on 121 tasks, under three conditions: no extra guidance / documentation (CodeWiki) / norm package (RepoNorm). All norms: 65.6 / 65.7 / 72.6. Contribution norms: 33.8 / 34.8 / 49.2. Behavioural norms: 96.5 / 95.5 / 96.0. Norms not stated in the task: 52.1 / 52.4 / 61.3. Main trends: behavioural norms are followed almost always (about 95-96%) whatever the help, while contribution norms are followed least (about a third without the package). The norm package gives the highest rate for all norms, contribution norms and unstated norms, with the biggest rise for contribution norms (33.8 to 49.2, about 15 points); documentation makes almost no difference (changes of under 1 point). For behavioural norms the three conditions are almost equal, with no help marginally highest.
